newsitem.title: USA: All is quiet on the U.S. Gulf foreign crude front.
newsitem.headline: All is quiet on the U.S. Gulf foreign crude front.

text.p: The waiting game surrounding renewed Iraqi oil exports, a volatile expiry for August NYMEX gasoline and an industry outing in Houston kept a tight lid on activity in the U.S. foreign crude market, traders said.
"It's been remarkably quiet," said one trader.
Additionally, some said most refiners have met their buying needs for August delivery to the Gulf Coast notwithstanding a number of outstanding offers.

Brent on a delivered basis by around mid-September was pegged by sellers at the price of September West Texas Intermediate, with the September spread between WTI and Brent still around $1.20 a barrel--even with Tuesday afternoon.

Still, one player was said to have sold an unspecified West African cargo for U.S. Gulf Coast delivery in the first 10 days of August at an undisclosed price. Some speculated it was Nigerian Qua Iboe, but that could not be confirmed.
Also, a West European oil company was said to have moved an Angolan Palanca cargo late Wednesday arriving in the September 15-20 window. The price could not be immediately confirmed.

On the South African front, players were not able to confirm that any Colombian Cusiana had moved Thursday, and the latest bombing of the Cano Limon pipeline was taken in stride as a way of life that had lost its ability to excite markets.

Also, the 960,000-barrel purchase tender by Chile's state oil refiner Empresa Nacional del Petroleo (ENAP) was still outstanding, with information on the tender not yet trickling into the market. Bids on the tender, which is due to arrive September 16-20, were due Thursday and traders expect to know Among the straggling August offers were several Nigerian cargoes such as Brass River as well as Argentine Canadon Seco.
A U.S. refiner was also heard to be re-selling 300,000 barrels of Zaire crude, asking September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing minus $1.00 a barrel for prompt delivery.
September pickings were also piling up. Several companies continued to gauge buying interest for North Sea Brent despite the somewhat tight trans-Atlantic arbitrage.
